subject: Lyon (1969)
object: Lyon (1969) reported an ultrastructural (electron microscopic) study of a nerve biopsy from a patient with early infantile chronic neuropathy.

subject: Ono et al. (1982)
object: Ono et al. (1982) described a 3-year 11-month-old Japanese boy with congenital hypomyelination. He had delayed motor development, generalized muscle hypotonia and weakness, and absent tendon reflexes due to peripheral neuropathy. His mental development was normal. Nerve conduction velocities could not be measured.

subject: Ono et al. (1982)
object: In the same patient, Ono et al. (1982) found on right sural nerve biopsy that most myelinated fibers had no myelin at all. Electron microscopy showed onion bulbs around the fibers, formed by concentric double-layered sheets of basement membrane with fragments of Schwann cell cytoplasm. The authors noted that these features were similar to previously reported cases.

subject: Charnas et al. (1988)
object: Charnas et al. (1988) described an infant born at 37 weeks' gestation who had lethal arthrogryposis multiplex congenita caused by complete absence of peripheral nervous system myelin. Supernumerary Schwann cells (onion bulbs) were not found.

subject: Charnas et al. (1988)
object: In this patient, Charnas et al. (1988) found that Schwann cells proliferated, migrated, ensheathed axons, produced basal lamina and then stopped proliferating normally, but they failed in spiral lengthening and longitudinal growth. The distance between Schwann cell nuclei was very short, giving marked Schwann cell hypercellularity, and the Schwann cells took on many morphologic features of unmyelinated nerves. Immunocytochemistry detected none of the PNS myelin proteins P0, P1 or MAG. The authors concluded that the defect appeared to be an arrest in Schwann cell differentiation at the stages of mesaxon elongation and longitudinal growth.

subject: Warner et al. (1996)
object: Warner et al. (1996) identified 5 novel mutations in the MPZ gene, which encodes the major structural protein (P0) of peripheral nerve myelin, in patients with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1B, Dejerine-Sottas syndrome, or congenital hypomyelination.

subject: Warner et al. (1996)
object: Warner et al. (1996) suggested that CMT1B, Dejerine-Sottas syndrome, and congenital hypomyelination may not be distinct pathophysiologic entities. Instead, they proposed that these disorders form a spectrum of related 'myelinopathies' caused by an underlying defect in myelination.

subject: Warner et al. (1996)
object: Warner et al. (1996) hypothesized that the differences in clinical severity seen with MPZ mutations depend on the type of mutation and its effect on protein function, that is, loss of function versus a dominant-negative effect.

subject: Tachi et al. (1998)
object: Tachi et al. (1998) described a male patient with a Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype. Sural nerve biopsy showed hypomyelinated fibers without active demyelination, and onion-bulb formations made of two parallel layers of basement membrane. This pathology was consistent with congenital hypomyelination neuropathy (CHN), but his clinical features were more severe than those of previously reported CHN patients.

subject: Tachi et al. (1998)
object: In a male patient with a Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype and nerve pathology consistent with CHN, Tachi et al. (1998) identified a GGCA insertion at nucleotide 560 of the MPZ (Po) gene. The insertion was a small direct tandem duplication in exon 4, which encodes the transmembrane domain. It shifted the reading frame and created a stop codon. The mutation was not found in either parent, and the authors suggested that mutation of the transmembrane domain probably has the largest impact on Po function.

subject: Phillips et al. (1999)
object: Phillips et al. (1999) reported long-term prospective follow-up of 2 unrelated girls with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. The first presented with neonatal hypotonia and extremely slow nerve conduction velocities, and sural nerve biopsy showed profound hypomyelination without inflammation or myelin breakdown. At age 9 years her motor function was still improving, but follow-up nerve conduction velocities had not changed.

subject: Phillips et al. (1999)
object: Phillips et al. (1999) described a second girl with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy who presented with hypotonia at age 5 months. Her nerve conduction velocities were extremely slow, and sural nerve biopsy showed severe hypomyelination without inflammation or myelin breakdown. At age 5 years her motor function had improved, but repeat nerve conduction velocities had not changed. Both patients had normal cognitive development.

subject: Phillips et al. (1999)
object: Phillips et al. (1999) found a point mutation in the myelin protein zero gene (MPZ) in their second patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. The same mutation had been reported in 3 other patients diagnosed with Dejerine-Sottas syndrome but never in a patient with CHN. The authors suggested that CHN, although a distinct clinical entity, may share similar genetic features with DSS.

subject: MPZ point mutation in the myelin protein zero gene
Mandich et al. (1999)
object: Mandich et al. (1999) described the clinical, morphologic, and immunohistochemical features of a patient with congenital hypomyelination (CH). CH is a hereditary demyelinating peripheral neuropathy with onset in early infancy, distal muscle weakness, hypotonia, areflexia, and severely slowed nerve conduction velocities. The authors noted that the patient's clinical features were quite distinct from those of CMT1B or Dejerine-Sottas syndrome.

subject: Mandich et al. (1999)
object: Mandich et al. (1999) identified a de novo Q215X mutation in the MPZ gene in a patient with congenital hypomyelination. The authors concluded that this confirmed CH is allelic with disorders that have a milder phenotype and a different clinical and neuropathologic profile, such as CMT1B and Dejerine-Sottas syndrome.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) generated transgenic mice carrying extra copies of the myelin protein zero gene (Mpz) and found that they manifested a dose-dependent dysmyelinating neuropathy ranging from transient perinatal hypomyelination to arrested myelination with impaired sorting of axons by Schwann cells; Mpz mRNA overexpression ranged from 30 to 700%.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) obtained ten transgenic founders with Mpz copy numbers ranging from 1 to more than 40; high copy number animals (F80.1, F80.8, F80.9, Tg80.2; copy number greater than 20) showed gait difficulty, reduced weight, tremor, atrophy of the paraspinal and hindlimb musculature and reduced life-span, with nerve conduction velocities profoundly reduced to about 2 m/s and temporal dispersion of the compound motor action potential, while leg muscles showed angulated and atrophic fibers suggestive of denervation without fiber type grouping.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) showed by semi-thin section and electron microscopic analysis of P28 sciatic nerve from high copy number Tg80.2 mice remarkable hypomyelination with an increased number of Schwann cell nuclei, no onion bulbs, bundles of unsorted naked axons of mixed caliber in every transverse section, Schwann cells surrounded by pockets of redundant basal lamina containing collagen, and little evidence of active demyelination or axonal degeneration.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) concluded that the dysmyelination resulted from developmental delay rather than myelin destruction: Tg80.2 sciatic nerves contained virtually no myelin at P5 and P14, fewer than 1% of axons in a 1:1 relationship with Schwann cells were myelinated in the P10 quadriceps nerve versus virtually 100% in wild type, and the motor branch was more dysmyelinated than the sensory branch of the femoral nerve.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) demonstrated that severity of dysmyelination paralleled Mpz dosage: mice with 0-10 copies (Tg80.3, 0.3-fold overexpression) were behaviorally normal with normally myelinated nerves at P28, mice with 10-20 copies (Tg80.4, 0.8-fold) had mild tremor, a nerve conduction velocity of 11 m/s and about 50% of large axons unmyelinated, and mice with more than 20 copies (Tg80.2, 7.3-fold) had evident tremor, weak grip strength, conduction velocity of 2 m/s and severe hypomyelination with delayed axonal sorting.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) placed the threshold for dysmyelination between 30 and 80% Mpz overexpression (130-180% total Mpz expression) by breeding the mildly affected Tg80.3 line to homozygosity, which raised overexpression from 30% to 80% and produced tremor and dysmyelination, and by crossing Tg80.4 into the homozygous Mpz null background, in which myelination returned to essentially normal, showing that the phenotype depended uniquely on Mpz dosage rather than on an ectopic effect or structural alteration of the transgenic P0.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) found by Western blot analysis that P0 overexpression dysregulated other myelin proteins even in the absence of dysmyelination: in P28 Tg80.3 nerves with ultrastructurally normal myelin, P0 was overexpressed by about 60% while MBP was reduced by about 50% and PMP22 by 35%, with tubulin unchanged; they concluded that Schwann cells sense and respond to P0 overexpression by dysregulating other myelin proteins before exceeding the threshold for dysmyelination.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) noted that the profoundly reduced nerve conduction velocities (1-2 m/s), the paucity of active myelin destruction or onion bulbs, and the redundant basement membrane formation in the P0 overexpressor mice resembled human congenital hypomyelination neuropathy (CHN), and that low-level P0 overexpression produced transient hypomyelination similar to a subset of reversible CHN; they suggested that P0 overexpression represents a new mechanism of hereditary neuropathy and that MPZ overexpression might contribute to the pathogenesis of the EGR2 mutation that likely disinhibits Krox 20.

subject: Wrabetz et al. (2000)
object: Wrabetz et al. (2000) advised caution regarding replacement gene therapy for CMT1B neuropathies in which the MPZ mutation predicts loss of P0 expression, noting that such therapy may require exceptionally precise regulation of P0 expression in human nerve because only 60% overexpression in mice resulted in impaired myelin formation.

subject: Szigeti et al. (2003)
object: Szigeti et al. (2003) reported a patient with congenital hypomyelination associated with cranial nerve dysfunction, respiratory failure, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the last confounding the clinical picture. Muscle biopsy findings suggested an effect of abnormal innervation on early postnatal muscle fiber differentiation.

subject: Szigeti et al. (2003)
object: In a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy, Szigeti et al. (2003) identified a complex de novo mutation in the MPZ gene consisting of a 3-bp deletion of CTA from nucleotides 550 to 552 and insertion of G at nucleotide 550, predicted by conceptual translation to result in a frameshift.

subject: MPZ 3bp deletion of CTA from nucleotide 550 to 552 and insertion of G at nucleotide 550
Nowakowski and Kochański (2004)
object: Nowakowski and Kochański (2004) screened the MPZ coding and promoter sequences in patients with CMT1, CMT2 and congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy (CHN), using SSCP and heteroduplex analysis. They found a T124K substitution in MPZ in 1 patient with CHN.

subject: Nowakowski and Kochański (2004)
object: Nowakowski and Kochański (2004) found the E56K mutation in MPZ in 1 family with axonal CMT (CMT2). They concluded that MPZ screening should be done across a wide range of CMT phenotypes.

subject: Kochanski et al. (2004)
object: Kochanski et al. (2004) identified a novel Thr124Lys mutation in the MPZ gene in a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy.

subject: Kochanski et al. (2004)
object: Kochanski et al. (2004) described the clinical and morphologic features of a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy, a severe neuropathy with early infancy onset in which sural nerve biopsy characteristically shows nonmyelinated and poorly myelinated axons with basal lamina onion bulbs and lack of myelin breakdown products.

subject: Smit et al. (2008)
object: Smit et al. (2008) described a family with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy in which a heterozygous mutation in the MPZ gene was confirmed in two generations.

subject: Smit et al. (2008)
object: Smit et al. (2008) noted that congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy is a rare condition with prenatal, neonatal, or early infantile onset of hypotonia, paresis, and areflexia. Histopathology shows absent or thin myelin sheaths, and most of the few reported patients die within the first years of life. Mutations had been described in the MPZ, EGR2, PMP22, and MTMR2 genes.

subject: NEUROPATHY, CONGENITAL HYPOMYELINATING, 2
object: MPZ 3bp deletion of CTA from nucleotide 550 to 552 and insertion of G at nucleotide 550
